'''Artur Konrad Ekert''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}} (born 19 September 1961) is a British-Polish physicist. He is a professor of [[quantum physics]] at the Mathematical Institute, [[Oxford University|University of Oxford]], professorial fellow in quantum physics and cryptography at [[Merton College, Oxford]], [[Lee Kong Chian]] Centennial Professor at the [[National University of Singapore]] and the founding director of the [[Centre for Quantum Technologies|Centre for Quantum Technologies (CQT)]]. His research interests extend over most aspects of information processing in quantum-mechanical systems, with a focus on [[quantum communication]] and [[quantum computation]]. He is best known as one of the pioneers of [[quantum cryptography]].

==Early life==
Ekert was born in [[Wrocław]], and studied physics at the [[Jagiellonian University]] in [[Kraków]] and at the University of Oxford. Between 1987 and 1991 he was a graduate student at [[Wolfson College, Oxford]]. In his doctoral thesis<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=DPhil|publisher=University of Oxford|title=Correlations in quantum optics|first= Artur Konrad|last=Ekert|year=1991|url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.293479|oclc=556450608}}</ref><ref name=mathgene/> he showed how [[quantum entanglement]] and non-locality can be used to distribute cryptographic keys with perfect security.

==Career==
In 1991, he was elected a junior research [[Oxbridge Fellow|fellow]] and subsequently (1994) a research fellow at [[Merton College, Oxford]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://fet11.ercim.eu/programme-and-exhibition/keynote-speakers|title=Keynote Speakers|publisher=FET11 / ERCIM|website=fet11.ercim.eu|access-date=2026-10-14}}</ref> At the time, he established the first research group in quantum cryptography and computation, based in the [[Clarendon Laboratory]], Oxford. Subsequently, it evolved into the [[Centre for Quantum Computation]], now based at [[Faculty of Mathematics, University of Cambridge]] in Cambridge.{{cn|date=October 2026}}

Between 1993 and 2000, he held a position of the [[Royal Society]] Howe Fellow. In 1998 he was appointed a professor of physics at the University of Oxford and a fellow and tutor in physics at [[Keble College, Oxford]]. From 2002 until 2006 he was the Leigh-Trapnell Professor of Quantum Physics at the [[Faculty of Mathematics, University of Cambridge|Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics]], [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge University]]<ref name="CV2015">{{cite web |url=https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/users/cvs/CVRS2015_0.pdf |title=CV Artur Ekert |work=maths.ox.ac.uk |date=2015 |access-date=2023-01-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230108112157/https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/system/files/users/cvs/CVRS2015_0.pdf |archive-date=2023-01-08}}</ref> and a professorial fellow of [[King's College, Cambridge]]. Since 2006 he has been a professor of quantum physics at the [[Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/people/artur.ekert |title=Prof Artur Ekert FRS |work=maths.ox.ac.uk |access-date=2024-01-11}}</ref> Also in 2006 he was appointed a Lee Kong Chian Centennial Professor at the National University of Singapore<ref name="CV2015"/> and became the founding director of the [[Centre for Quantum Technologies]] (CQT). After retiring from the director position in 2020, he remains a ''Distinguished Fellow'' at CQT.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.quantumlah.org/research/group/Artur-Ekert |title=Artur Ekert Group |work=quantumlah.org |access-date=2024-01-11}}</ref> In 2020, he joined the [[Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology]] as an ''adjunct professor''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://groups.oist.jp/po/2020-year-end-letter-peter-gruss |title=2020 Year-End Letter from Peter Gruss |work=oist.jp |date=2020 |access-date=2024-01-11}}</ref>

He has worked with and advised several companies and government agencies, served on various professional advisory boards, and is the Vice Chairman of The Noel Croucher Foundation.<ref>{{cite web
| url        = http://www.croucher.org.hk/category/board-of-trustees
| title      = Board of Trustees
| author     = <!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->
| work = Croucher Foundation
| date       = 2015
| access-date = 28 January 2016
}}
</ref>

==Research==
Ekert's research extends over most aspects of information processing in quantum-mechanical systems, with a focus on quantum cryptography and quantum computation. Building on the idea of quantum non-locality and Bell's inequalities <ref>{{cite book
| last = Bell
| first = John Stuart
| title = Speakable and Unspeakable in Quantum Mechanics
| year = 2004
| publisher = Cambridge University Press
| isbn = 0-521-52338-9}}</ref> 
he introduced entanglement-based quantum key distribution. His 1991 paper<ref>{{cite journal
| last       = Ekert
| first      = Artur
| date       = 5 August 1991
| title      = Quantum cryptography based on Bell's theorem
| journal    = Physical Review Letters
| publisher  = American Physical Society
| volume     = 67
| issue = 6
| pages      = 661–663
| doi        = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.67.661
|bibcode = 1991PhRvL..67..661E
| pmid=10044956| s2cid = 27683254
}}
</ref> generated a spate of new research that established a vigorously active new area of [[physics]] and [[cryptography]]. It is one of the most cited papers in the field and was chosen by the editors of the ''[[Physical Review Letters]]'' as one of their "milestone letters", i.e., papers that made important contributions to physics, announced significant discoveries, or started new areas of research. His subsequent work with [[John Rarity]] and Paul Tapster, from the [[Defence Research Agency]] (DRA) in Malvern, resulted in the proof-of-principle experimental quantum key distribution, introducing parametric down-conversion, phase encoding, and quantum interferometry into the repertoire of cryptography.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1       = Ekert
| first1      = Artur
| last2      = Rarity
| first2     = John G.
| last3      = Tapster
| first3     = Paul R.
| last4      = Palma
| first4     = G. Massimo
| date       = 31 August 1992
| title      = Practical quantum cryptography based on two-photon interferometry
| journal    = Physical Review Letters
| publisher  = American Physical Society
| volume     = 69
| issue = 9
| pages      = 1293–1295
| doi        = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.1293
|bibcode = 1992PhRvL..69.1293E
| pmid=10047180}}
</ref>
He and collaborators were the first to develop the concept of a security proof based on entanglement purification.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1       = Deutsch
| first1      = David
| last2      = Ekert
| first2     = Artur
| last3      = Jozsa
| first3     = Richard
| last4      = Macchiavello
| first4     = Chiara
| last5      = Popescu
| first5     = Sandu
| last6      = Sanpera
| first6     = Anna
| date       = 23 September 1996
| title      = Quantum privacy amplification and the security of quantum cryptography over noisy channels
| journal    = Physical Review Letters
| publisher  = American Physical Society
| volume     = 77
| issue = 13
| pages      = 2818–2821
| doi        = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.2818
|arxiv = quant-ph/9604039 |bibcode = 1996PhRvL..77.2818D
 | pmid=10062053| s2cid = 2765155
}}
</ref>

Ekert and colleagues have made a number of contributions to both theoretical aspects of quantum computation and proposals for its experimental realisations. These include proving that almost any quantum logic gate operating on two quantum bits is universal,<ref>{{cite journal
| last1       = Deutsch
| first1      = David
| last2      = Barenco
| first2     = Adriano
| last3      = Ekert
| first3     = Artur
| date       = 8 June 1995
| title      = Universality in quantum computation
| journal    = Proceedings of the Royal Society A
| volume     = 449
| issue      = 1937
| pages      = 669–677
| doi        = 10.1098/rspa.1995.0065
|arxiv = quant-ph/9505018 |bibcode = 1995RSPSA.449..669D | s2cid = 15088854
}}
</ref> proposing one of the first realistic implementations of quantum computation, e.g. using the induced dipole-dipole coupling in an optically driven array of [[quantum dots]],<ref>{{cite journal
| last1       = Barenco
| first1      = Adriano
| last2      = Deutsch
| first2     = David
| last3      = Ekert
| first3     = Artur
| last4      = Jozsa
| first4     = Richard
| date       = 15 May 1995
| title      = Conditional quantum dynamics and logic gates
| journal    = Physical Review Letters
| volume     = 74
| issue = 20
| pages      = 4083–4086
| doi        = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.4083
| pmid = 10058408
|arxiv = quant-ph/9503017 |bibcode = 1995PhRvL..74.4083B | s2cid = 26611140
}}
</ref> introducing more stable geometric quantum logic gates,<ref>{{cite journal
| last1       = Jones
| first1      = Jonathan A.
| last2      = Vedral
| first2     = Vlatko
| last3      = Ekert
| first3     = Artur
| last4      = Castagnoli
| first4     = Giuseppe
| date       = 24 February 2000
| title      = Geometric quantum computation using nuclear magnetic resonance
| journal    = Nature
| volume     = 403
| issue = 6772
| pages      = 869–871
| doi        = 10.1038/35002528
| pmid = 10706278
|arxiv = quant-ph/9910052 |bibcode = 2000Natur.403..869J | s2cid = 4415368
}}
</ref> and proposing "noiseless encoding", which became later known as decoherence-free subspaces.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1       = Palma
| first1      = G. Massimo
| last2      = Suominen
| first2     = Kalle-Antti
| last3      = Ekert
| first3     = Artur
| date       = 8 March 1996
| title      = Quantum computers and dissipation
| journal    = Proceedings of the Royal Society A
| volume     = 452
| issue      = 1946
| pages      = 567–584
| doi        = 10.1098/rspa.1996.0029
|arxiv = quant-ph/9702001 |bibcode = 1996RSPSA.452..567P | s2cid = 17240058
}}
</ref>

His other notable contributions include work on quantum state swapping, optimal quantum state estimation and quantum state transfer. With some of the same collaborators, he has written on connections between the notion of mathematical proofs and the laws of physics.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1       = Deutsch
| first1      = David
| last2      = Ekert
| first2     = Artur
| last3      = Lupacchini
| first3     = Rossella
| date       = September 2000
| title      = Machines, logic and quantum physics
| journal    = The Bulletin of Symbolic Logic
| publisher  = Cambridge University Press
| volume     = 6
| issue      = 3
| pages      = 265–283
| doi        = 10.2307/421056
| jstor = 421056
| arxiv= math/9911150
| s2cid = 6658624
}}
</ref> He has also contributed semi-popular writing on the history of science.<ref>{{cite journal
| last       = Ekert
| first      = Artur
| date       = August 2008
| title      = Complex and unpredictable Cardano
| journal    = International Journal of Theoretical Physics
| publisher  = Springer
| volume     = 47
| issue      = 8
| pages      = 2101–2119
| doi        = 10.1007/s10773-008-9775-1
|arxiv = 0806.0485 |bibcode = 2008IJTP...47.2101E | s2cid = 6067361
}}
</ref>

==Honours and awards==
For his discovery of quantum cryptography he was awarded the 1995 [[Maxwell Medal and Prize]] by the [[Institute of Physics]], the 2007 [[Hughes Medal]] by the Royal Society, the 2019 [[Micius Quantum Prize]] and the 2024 Royal Society [[Milner Award]]. He is also a co-recipient of the 2004 [[European Union]] [[Descartes Prize]]. In 2016 he was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]].<ref name=frs/> He is a fellow of the Singapore National Academy of Science and a recipient of the 2017 Singapore Public Administration Medal (Silver) [[Pingat Pentadbiran Awam]]. He is a foreign member of the [[Polish Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. In 2025 he was awarded the Commander's Cross of the [[Order of Polonia Restituta]].
